summary.text: 喝 combines 口, a mouth-related meaning element, with 曷, traditionally assigned the sound role. It is used for drinking and also for hoarseness and calling or scolding; the record does not establish how these senses relate.

formation.text: The received analysis is phonosemantic: 口 marks a mouth-related category, while 曷 supplies a sound cue. This traditional account does not independently establish the graph’s original formation.

components.text: 口 marks the mouth-related category in the traditional analysis. No pictured scene or earlier graphic form for 喝 is established.
曷 is assigned the phonetic role; its question-word meanings do not explain 喝. The reported sound comparison is broad: 喝 has multiple reconstructed readings, not all matching 曷 in the same way.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison is reported through a secondary source, and no primary reconstruction table for 曷 was checked. Multiple readings of 喝 mean it cannot be treated as one uniform pronunciation history.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang’s Old Chinese system, 曷 is reported as *ɡaːd; 喝 is reported with *qʰaːd, *qraːds, and *qʰoːb. These reconstructions suggest broad sound-series context, not an identical match across readings.
sound.system: Old Chinese, Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003), as reported by a secondary reference

history.text: The received Shuowen entry analyzes 喝 as 口 plus phonetic 曷 and glosses it with 㵣. The selected seal-script-style image illustrates this traditional analysis; it is a modern redraw, not a dated artifact or evidence of an evolutionary sequence.

The cited records provide no readable oracle-bone, bronze, or manuscript forms and establish no sequence of graphic changes or corruption. The seal-style image therefore cannot establish the earliest shape.

uncertainties.text: A relationship between 喝 and the separate drinking graph 欱 has been proposed, but the available evidence does not establish borrowing, replacement spelling, or another historical pathway. No object-name or pictured referent is established for an object-name borrowing account.

The drinking, hoarseness, and calling or scolding senses are recorded, but their earliest attestations and any chronological development between them remain unresolved. The proposed original sense “thirsty” is not independently confirmed.

evidence.text: mouth
Phonosemantic compound. 口 represents the meaning and 曷 represents the sound.
㵣也。从口曷聲。

Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *qraːds, *qʰoːb, *qʰaːd): semantic 口 (“mouth”) + phonetic 曷 (OC *ɡaːd).
An innovative written form of 欱 (MC xop), from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *hwap (“to drink”). Cognate to 噏 (OC *qʰrub, “to drink”) and 呷 (OC *qʰraːb, “to drink”) (Schuessler, 2007).
Compare Burmese ဟစ် (hac, “to call out loudly”) (Luce, 1981).
㵣也。从口曷聲。

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing the Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The entry gives “㵣也。从口曷聲” (“[㵣] also; from 口, with 曷 as phonetic”). Duan Yucai comments that a pronunciation note may have been omitted and cites older literary uses of 喝 for hoarseness or a hoarse voice. This supports a traditional phonosemantic analysis, but Shuowen is a historical lexicographic account rather than independent proof of the character’s original formation.
evidence.title: 說文解字「喝」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 喝: Shuowen forms, readings, senses, and source inventory
evidence.text: The dictionary transcribes the Great Xu edition’s definition and Duan edition’s explicit “从口，曷聲,” and records Mandarin readings hē, hè, yè. It associates hē with drinking; hè with scolding, calling aloud, and an exclamatory use; and yè with a hoarse or constricted voice. It cites 《論衡·氣壽》 and 《後漢書·張酺傳》 for hoarseness and 《舊唐書·哥舒翰列傳》 for a scolding use. Its listed oracle-bone and bronze-script reference collections are marked unavailable, so this inspected entry does not establish early graphic forms or a corruption sequence.
evidence.title: A00625 喝 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 欱: definition, composition, and cited use
evidence.text: 欱 is independently described in Shuowen as “歠也。从欠，合聲” (to drink/sip; from 欠 with 合 as phonetic), with the reading 呼合切. The dictionary glosses it as drinking or sucking and cites Zhang Heng’s Western Capital Rhapsody. This establishes an old drinking graph and a lexical parallel, but does not by itself establish that 喝 historically replaced or borrowed 欱.
evidence.title: B01915 欱 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Wiktionary Chinese entry for 喝, reporting Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)
evidence.field: 喝: reconstructed pronunciations and phonetic-series comparison
evidence.text: The entry reports three Old Chinese reconstructions for 喝 in Zhengzhang’s system: *qraːds, *qʰoːb, and *qʰaːd, corresponding to separate readings; its phonetic-series table gives 曷 *ɡaːd. It reports Middle Chinese xat for the 入聲 reading and an OC *qʰoːb reading corresponding to 欱. These are source-reported reconstructions, not directly observed ancient pronunciations. The diversity of readings cautions against treating modern hē as the sole historical pronunciation or requiring every reading to match 曷 identically.

The matching hē-style reading and drinking gloss make a relationship with the drinking use of 喝 plausible, but the source does not show that the name of any depicted object explains the sound. evidence.field: 喝: form record, Shuowen analysis, readings, meanings, and cited early uses
evidence.text: The entry displays one small-seal example, no examples under bronze, oracle-bone, or bamboo-and-silk headings, and four examples under “other.” It transmits the Shuowen analysis “㵣也。从口，曷聲” and records Guangyun fanqie readings 於犗 and 許葛, respectively Middle Chinese level descriptors for departing-tone grade-two and entering-tone grade-one readings. Its account proposes the original sense “thirsty,” now associated with 渴, and lists examples of hoarseness in Sima Xiangru’s “Zixu fu” and Wang Chong’s Lunheng, and calling aloud in Jin Shu. Those are source assertions and cited textual examples, not independently verified first attestations; the page does not date the small-seal glyph to an excavated artifact.

gaps: No inspected paleographic corpus supplied readable oracle-bone, bronze, or manuscript forms for 喝; the MOE dictionary lists the relevant paleographic reference sets but marks them unavailable. Therefore the earliest attested graph form, graphic development, and any graphic corruption remain unresolved.

Shuowen records 喝 as 㵣 with components 口 and 曷, but its own gloss is difficult to interpret and does not establish the character's original sense. No independent early inscriptional evidence was found to confirm or overturn that account.

The inspected sources document a Han-era hoarseness sense, a Guangyun hoarseness reading, and later historical scolding/calling examples. They do not provide a dated earliest attestation for the drinking use of 喝, nor demonstrate a chronological semantic path among drinking, hoarseness, and shouting.

欱 is an independently attested drinking graph analyzed as 欠 plus phonetic 合. The proposed relationship to 喝 (loan, replacement spelling, or another lexical relation) requires earlier dated text examples and phonological analysis that were not obtained. An OC reconstruction associated with 喝’s 欱-like reading does not on its own prove the name or pronunciation of any depicted object.

No primary reconstruction table for 曷 was directly queried in this session. Zhengzhang OC values are reported by the opened Wiktionary entry; system, period, and variant readings are specified there, but should be checked against the 2003 work before fine-grained phonetic claims.

The dossier’s Burmese comparison and Proto-Sino-Tibetan *hwap proposal were not independently verified from an inspected primary comparative source. The database excerpts and online dictionary templates are not enough to establish cognacy.

No evidence was found that an original pictured weapon, tool, or object is involved in 喝’s proposed phonetic borrowing. Its sound-component analysis does not require recovering such a referent; that question is separate from the unresolved proposed whole-word relationship with 欱.

No inspected excavated oracle-bone, bronze, or manuscript form of 喝 was located. The observed seal-style image is a modern redraw and cannot establish an ancient artifact form, earliest attestation, or graphic chronology.

No source inspected here demonstrates a sequence of graphic changes or corruption in 喝. The Shuowen component analysis is a historical dictionary account; it is not independent proof of original formation.

The CUHK entry proposes an original sense of thirst and later senses including hoarseness and calling, but the cited texts were not checked in editions with dates, and they do not establish a semantic chronology. Earliest attestation of the drink sense and links among the senses remain unsettled.

The relation of 喝 to the independent drinking graph 欱 remains a lexical hypothesis in the supplied dossier. The reported reconstruction associated with the 欱-like reading does not establish an object-name borrowing, nor was a source word or pictured object's name independently recovered.

Zhengzhang reconstructions were inspected only through a secondary dictionary page. No primary reconstruction table was checked here; the entries have multiple reading variants, so broad phonetic-series compatibility should not be mistaken for a single pronunciation history.
Burmese and Proto-Sino-Tibetan comparisons in the supplied dossier were not independently verified in this web stage. No conclusions about cognacy are added.

items.period: Seal-script style, represented as the Shuowen seal form; precise artifact date not supplied
items.tradition: Chinese small seal script style; modern digital redraw
items.caption: This seal-script-style form of 喝 is presented in connection with the Shuowen analysis “from 口, with 曷 as phonetic.” It illustrates that received analysis, not a directly dated ancient inscription.
items.alt: Black seal-script-style glyph 喝 on a white background, with 口 on the left and 曷 on the right.
items.selection_reason: The visible form is legible, and its seal-script style provides an illustration of the traditional component account. It is a modern redraw, so it cannot establish the character’s earliest form or graphic development.
items.rights: Public domain release of the digital SVG representation, as stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: This image is a modern redraw of a seal-script-style form, not a dated artifact. Early graphic forms and any sequence of graphic changes remain unresolved in the inspected evidence.

The traditional account assigns 曷 a phonetic role and 口 a semantic role, but it does not independently prove how 喝 originated. The image alone cannot establish the character’s meaning, pronunciation, or historical development.
